# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

</document>
response:
# Critical Reading: Achterberg et al., Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

This is the most balanced of the four documents. The protocol was registered, self-rated productivity was excluded, and actual hours were used where available. The review also examines exactly the moderators the earlier documents identified: study design, the hours measure, the output measure and the type of work. It reports a prediction interval, admits that its moderators overlap, and rejects both extremes: Halden's "sector-general" and Varga and Holm's "entirely an artifact."

The numbers are internally consistent. The confidence intervals are symmetric on the log scale, as the stated method requires. Subgroup counts add to 23 in each grouping. The per-hour and per-worker estimates imply plausible hours reductions of roughly 11–15%.

Two conclusions go beyond the evidence: the dismissal of novelty effects, and the reading of the bias-adjusted and subgroup estimates as independent agreement. There are also some methodological gaps that matter given the earlier documents.

## 1. The duration conclusion is the review's main overreach

> "Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside."

This rests on four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, compared with the other nineteen. That evidence cannot carry the conclusion:

- **It compares studies, not time points.** Decay is a change within a study over time. Comparing long studies with short ones confounds duration with everything else that differs between them, including design, sector and the measures used. Within-study trajectories, such as the output at 6 months and at 18 months in the same organisations, are what would show decay.
- **Long follow-up selects for success.** Organisations that reverted, like Halden's five or its nine withdrawals, don't produce 18-month data. The long-run studies are probably survivors of survivors.
- **The design of the four studies is not reported.** If they are mostly uncontrolled or use scheduled hours, their +14.0% is inflated in the same way as the uncontrolled estimate (+18.7%). If so, matching the pooled +13.4% would be compatible with *some* decay from a higher starting point.
- **The interval is wide.** At +6.2% to +22.4%, it cannot rule out meaningful decay.

This mirrors Varga and Holm's mistake in the opposite direction. They asserted novelty from two survey points. The review dismisses it using four studies that are not comparable with the rest. The defensible statement is that longer studies have not shown obvious decay, and that within-study evidence is lacking. Varden's 24-month follow-up will be more informative than this comparison.

## 2. The "convergence on 8–10%" is not independent corroboration

The discussion says controlled studies, actual-hours studies, record-based studies and the bias-adjusted estimate "converge" on roughly 8–10%. These are not four independent checks:

- **The subgroups overlap heavily.** 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of 14 used manager-reported output. The controlled, actual-hours and record-based subgroups are therefore largely the same studies viewed from different angles.
- **The small-study adjustment probably repeats the design correction.** Small studies are likely to be the uncontrolled, scheduled-hours, manager-reported pilots. Funnel asymmetry may reflect this real difference in design rather than publication bias. The review reads it as publication bias without considering the alternative. Egger's test and trim-and-fill are also known to be unreliable at I² = 81%.
- **The study with all three corrections is missing.** The relevant estimate is for studies that were controlled, measured actual hours *and* used record-based output, ideally randomised. The review doesn't report it. Its corrections may not add up straightforwardly, so the result could be lower or higher than 8%. With only three randomised studies, it should still be shown.

The range of 8–10% is plausible, and it fits Varden's +12.5% and Varga and Holm's +10.8%. But the review shows one finding several times, not several findings agreeing.

## 3. There is no risk-of-bias assessment, so attrition is invisible

The methods describe search, inclusion, coding and synthesis, but no risk-of-bias assessment, such as ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies and RoB 2 for the trials. That matters after Varga and Holm. Halden misreported seven of nine withdrawals as preparation-phase dropouts, and six of those cited workload. Other uncontrolled pilots may have done the same.

None of the review's moderators captures survivorship. The review also does not say whether Halden entered at its published +23.4% or at a corrected value. The rejection of Varga and Holm says the controlled subgroups "avoid the problems that re-analysis identified," but that holds only in part:

- **Attrition:** matched or difference-in-differences designs with volunteer organisations can still lose the strugglers.
- **Novelty:** this was Varga and Holm's main argument for the residual gain, and no subgroup avoids it. The review answers it only with the weak duration evidence in point 1.

The review's rejection of "entirely an artifact" is still sound on the measurement points. The controlled estimate (+4.0% to +12.6%) and the actual-hours estimate (+3.6% to +12.4%) both exclude zero, which matches what I concluded from Varden. The rejection is weaker on novelty.

## 4. Work type may be confounded with design

The controlled studies are "mostly in the public sector," and five of the nine are discretionary. That leaves up to four controlled studies among the seven coverage-bound and three mixed studies. Coverage-bound work may therefore be controlled at a higher rate (up to 57%) than discretionary work (38%).

If so, part of the per-hour gap between the two (+6.2% vs +15.1%) is a design effect. The review's restricted estimate supports this: controlled discretionary studies gave +9.6%, not +15.1%. The per-worker contrast is more robust (−8.9% vs −2.7% within controlled discretionary studies).

The meta-regression says all three moderators remain associated when included together. But that model has 23 studies and at least four parameters, with moderators the authors say they "cannot fully separate." The "58% explained" figure is likely to be optimistic.

## 5. The abstract leads with the less reliable figures

The abstract says per-worker output "fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%)." The +0.6% figure mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. The controlled discretionary figure is −2.7% (−6.5% to +1.2%), and controlled studies overall show −4.1% (−7.6% to −0.5%), an interval that excludes zero. The pooled −1.8% that the abstract reports alongside is held near zero mainly by the uncontrolled studies.

The discussion is more careful ("maintained or falling slightly"). The abstract should match it.

## 6. The coverage-bound per-hour gain may not be real productivity

The review calls the coverage-bound per-hour gain "real but too small to compensate." As with Varden's counter offices, when fewer staff face the same demand, utilisation rises: queues lengthen and idle time shrinks. Output per hour then rises without anyone working faster. The +6.2% may be partly this, plus longer waits for the public. The review would need service-quality outcomes, such as waits and abandonment, to tell the difference. It doesn't pool them.

## 7. Missing analyses

- **Dose-response.** Hours cuts range from 10% upwards, but the size of the cut is never used as a moderator. It is the obvious one, and it matters mechanically: with output held flat, a bigger cut produces a bigger per-hour gain.
- **Cost.** With pay maintained, output per worker is the inverse of unit labour cost. Even the controlled discretionary −2.7% implies higher cost per unit, before any paid overtime. For Varden's case-processing offices I estimated a rise of roughly 15–18%, which depended on assumed overtime terms. The review's discussion of "whether that gain is enough" stops short of this.
- **How multi-arm studies were handled.** Varden has two strata with opposite findings. The paper does not say whether it was split into two entries, coded as "mixed," or reduced to one estimate. Each choice affects the work-type moderator and the independence of estimates.

## 8. Mechanisms and wellbeing

- **Fatigue.** The r = 0.18 across 11 studies has a 95% interval from roughly −0.47 to +0.70. It is also an ecological correlation, between studies rather than within them. The review rightly doesn't draw a strong conclusion. It is consistent with fatigue being a weak explanation, but doesn't show it.
- **Meetings.** "Cannot assess" is the right call, and fairer to Varden than Varga and Holm were.
- **Sick leave.** "Fell in all 14 studies" is vote counting. The pooled −31% is subject to the issue I raised with Varden: where the shorter week is delivered as four days, a 20% fall in sick days is roughly mechanical. Pooling absence per scheduled day or per hour would resolve this.

## How the four documents fit together

| Question | Halden | Varden | Varga and Holm | Meta-analysis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, best estimate | +23.4% | +12.5% (case-processing) | +10.8% (survivors) | +8–10% (bias-adjusted/controlled) |
| Coverage-bound work | "Sector-general" | Output/FTE −11.4% | Agrees with Varden | Output/worker −8.9%, consistent |
| Novelty or decay | Not addressed | 9 months; 24-month follow-up under way | "Entirely" novelty (untested) | "Set aside" (weak evidence) |
| Mechanism | Fatigue | Meetings (exploratory) | Neither | Fatigue weak; meetings untestable |

## Bottom line

**Well supported:**
- Gains in output per actual hour are real but modest, probably in the high single digits to low teens, and about half the headline pilot figures.
- Study design and measurement choices substantially inflate uncontrolled estimates.
- Coverage-bound work loses about 9% of output per worker when staffing patterns are unchanged.
- "Sector-general" and "entirely an artifact" are both rejected.

**Overstated or under-examined:**
- That novelty "can be set aside," which rests on four studies compared across studies and probably skewed towards survivors.
- That the four routes to 8–10% are independent agreement, when they largely overlap.
- The absence of any risk-of-bias or attrition assessment, after attrition was shown to have been misreported in the largest included pilot.
- The abstract's per-worker framing for discretionary work, which uses the uncontrolled figure.
- The missing dose-response, cost and service-quality analyses.

**Questions still open across all four documents:**
- **Durability:** whether the gains persist, which needs within-study trajectories, Varden's 24-month results among them.
- **Mechanism:** whether the gains come from rest or from removing low-value time. This determines whether cutting hours is needed at all.
- **Cost:** whether the gains offset the higher cost per unit of output that comes with maintaining full pay.
